common_name: Eyriesii Easter Lily Cactus (Classic White Torch Cactus)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container specimen in full sun to bright light in fast-draining cactus mix; this classic globe-to-column species clusters into multi-headed clumps and needs a distinct winter rest with minimal water to trigger reliable spring flowering.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container specimen in full sun to bright light in fast-draining cactus mix; this classic globe-to-column species clusters into multi-headed clumps and needs a distinct winter rest with minimal water to trigger reliable spring flowering. The dark green, deeply ribbed stems are the archetype of the genus and the original species behind the common name 'Easter lily cactus,' producing huge, trumpet-shaped, fragrant white flowers on long tubes that open at night and last only a day or two. Native to Argentina and Uruguay, it is one of the hardiest and easiest Echinopsis to grow, tolerating light frost briefly if kept dry. Feed lightly during the growing season, water deeply then let the mix dry fully between waterings, and expect the heaviest bloom flush once the plant has formed a good-sized clustering clump.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

common_name: Rose Quartz Echinopsis (Pink Hybrid Flowering Cactus)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or patio container in full sun to bright light in fast-draining cactus mix; propagate this named hybrid only from offsets or cuttings, since seed will not reproduce the clone true to type.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or patio container in full sun to bright light in fast-draining cactus mix; propagate this named hybrid only from offsets or cuttings, since seed will not reproduce the clone true to type. 'Rose Quartz' belongs to the modern group of large-flowered Echinopsis hybrids bred from crosses among Echinopsis, Trichocereus, and Lobivia parentage, selected for oversized blooms that open in daylight and often persist longer than the fleeting night flowers of the wild species. Its clustering, spiny green stems stay compact while producing soft pink, many-petaled flowers 5 to 6 inches across in late spring and early summer. Keep the clump on the dry side through winter dormancy and resume regular watering as new flower buds swell in spring for the best repeat bloom.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

common_name: Los Angeles Echinopsis (Orange-Red Hybrid Flowering Cactus)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or patio container in full sun to bright light in fast-draining cactus mix; this named hybrid is propagated only by division or offset cuttings to keep its flower color true.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or patio container in full sun to bright light in fast-draining cactus mix; this named hybrid is propagated only by division or offset cuttings to keep its flower color true. One of the popular mid-20th-century large-flowered Echinopsis hybrids developed from crosses among Echinopsis, Trichocereus, and Lobivia species, 'Los Angeles' bears vivid orange-red, satiny flowers 4 to 6 inches wide that open during the day and can repeat over several weeks in late spring. The clumping, ribbed, spiny stems stay low and offset readily, forming a multi-headed mound over a few seasons. Provide a cool, dry winter rest to set flower buds, then increase water gradually as new growth and buds appear in spring.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Plant rooted columnar cuttings or nursery starts in full sun in extremely well-drained, sandy or gravelly soil; this fast-growing torch cactus needs staking or wall support while young until the base thickens enough to stay upright.

directions: Plant rooted columnar cuttings or nursery starts in full sun in extremely well-drained, sandy or gravelly soil; this fast-growing torch cactus needs staking or wall support while young until the base thickens enough to stay upright. Native to the Bolivian Andes, it forms tall, multi-ribbed, blue-green columns that branch from the base with age and are among the quicker-growing large columnar cacti in cultivation, adding a foot or more of height per year under good conditions. Large white, fragrant, night-blooming flowers open along the upper stems in summer, followed by edible fruit. Grow it as a striking accent or informal barrier planting in frost-free xeriscape gardens, and protect from prolonged wet, cold conditions, which quickly cause stem rot.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in full sun to bright light in fast-draining cactus mix; the dense, soft-looking white spine covering hides a plant that still needs a dry, cool winter rest to flower well.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in full sun to bright light in fast-draining cactus mix; the dense, soft-looking white spine covering hides a plant that still needs a dry, cool winter rest to flower well. Native to the high valleys of Bolivia, this small clustering species forms tight mounds of cylindrical stems so thickly covered in fine, silky white spines that it looks almost furry, giving rise to its common name. Clusters of pale yellow to soft salmon-orange flowers ring the base of the stems in mid-spring, opening in succession over several weeks. Keep almost completely dry from late fall through late winter, then resume regular watering once flower buds appear to avoid splitting the tightly packed offsets.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining cactus mix; this tiny clustering species offsets rapidly and is best grown in a wide, shallow pot to accommodate its spreading mats.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining cactus mix; this tiny clustering species offsets rapidly and is best grown in a wide, shallow pot to accommodate its spreading mats. Among the smallest cultivated Rebutia relatives, its pea-sized stems bear soft, bristly, whitish spines and multiply quickly into a low, dense carpet only an inch or two tall. In spring it produces a profusion of pure white to pale pink funnel-shaped flowers that can nearly cover the plant, unusual among Rebutia relatives that mostly flower orange or red. Give it a cool, dry winter rest, then water regularly through the growing season while avoiding standing moisture around the shallow, wide-spreading root system.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in full sun in fast-draining cactus mix; the tightly packed, starburst-like spine pattern needs bright direct light to stay dense and well colored.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in full sun in fast-draining cactus mix; the tightly packed, starburst-like spine pattern needs bright direct light to stay dense and well colored. Native to a small area of southern Bolivia, this dwarf clustering species has flattened, disc-like stems covered in radiating combs of fine golden-white spines pressed close to the body, one of the more striking spine patterns in the genus. Bright orange-red flowers emerge from the stem bases in spring, often nearly as large as the tiny plant body itself. Because the stems stay so flat and low, protect it from overhead watering that can pool around the crown, and keep it completely dry during its winter dormancy.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow in bright light to full sun in an extremely fast-draining, mineral succulent mix; withhold water completely while the old leaf pair is being reabsorbed each year to avoid splitting or rot.

directions: Grow in bright light to full sun in an extremely fast-draining, mineral succulent mix; withhold water completely while the old leaf pair is being reabsorbed each year to avoid splitting or rot. One of the most variable and widely grown Lithops species, it forms paired, fused, grayish to pale brown or pinkish-tan leaf bodies with a network of fine reddish dots and translucent surface markings that vary considerably between populations. A single white daisy-like flower opens from the fissure between the leaves in autumn, usually after the seasonal rest has ended and new leaves have started forming. Because so many named color forms exist, grow it in very lean soil and bright light to keep the body compact and richly marked rather than stretched and pale.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow in bright light to full sun in an extremely fast-draining, mineral succulent mix; one of the more heat- and drought-tolerant Lithops species, it still needs a fully dry rest while the old leaf pair shrivels.

directions: Grow in bright light to full sun in an extremely fast-draining, mineral succulent mix; one of the more heat- and drought-tolerant Lithops species, it still needs a fully dry rest while the old leaf pair shrivels. Widespread across Namibia and South Africa, it is one of the most common Lithops species in cultivation, with a thick, blunt-topped leaf pair in shades of gray, tan, or olive marked by a network of darker channels and dots forming a maze-like pattern on the flattened leaf faces. A solitary yellow flower opens from the central fissure in fall, typically emerging before the new leaf pair has fully replaced the old one. Its tolerance for a wide range of mineral soils and bright exposures makes it a good, reliable species for growers newer to living stones.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow in bright light to full sun in an extremely fast-draining, mineral succulent mix; the warm rust-and-orange leaf coloring intensifies with strong light and lean, mineral soil.

directions: Grow in bright light to full sun in an extremely fast-draining, mineral succulent mix; the warm rust-and-orange leaf coloring intensifies with strong light and lean, mineral soil. Native to South Africa's Northern Cape, this species is prized among living-stone growers for its warm reddish-brown to burnt-orange leaf tops patterned with darker branching channels, among the most vividly colored faces in the genus. A bright yellow flower opens from the leaf fissure in autumn, contrasting sharply against the warm-toned body. As with other Lithops, keep it completely dry while the old leaf pair is being consumed by new growth in late winter and spring, resuming water only once the old pair has fully dried to a papery husk.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow in very well-drained, mineral, gritty succulent mix in bright light rather than harsh direct summer sun, since this dark-colored form scorches more easily than green Lithops.

directions: Grow in very well-drained, mineral, gritty succulent mix in bright light rather than harsh direct summer sun, since this dark-colored form scorches more easily than green Lithops. 'Rubra' is a selectively bred color form of Lithops optica with deep maroon to purplish-red leaf bodies, a striking contrast to the pale gray-green of the typical species and one of the most sought-after living stones among collectors. It follows the same strict seasonal leaf-exchange cycle as other Lithops, with a single white to pale lavender flower opening from the leaf cleft in fall. Because its darker pigmentation absorbs more heat, give it slightly more shade during the hottest part of summer than other Lithops, and keep it bone-dry through the winter leaf transition.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to partial sun in fast-draining cactus mix; this small clustering species is one of the more shade-tolerant Gymnocalycium and can scorch in intense summer sun.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to partial sun in fast-draining cactus mix; this small clustering species is one of the more shade-tolerant Gymnocalycium and can scorch in intense summer sun. Native to the Cordoba hills of central Argentina, it forms small, rounded, dark green to bronze-green stems with low, notched ribs and offsets freely into tight clumps. It is notable among Gymnocalycium for its bright yellow flowers with a reddish throat, unlike the white or pink blooms typical of most relatives in the genus, opening from the crown in late spring and early summer. Water regularly through the growing season, then keep nearly dry over winter to encourage a strong flush of flowers the following year.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in full sun to bright light in fast-draining cactus mix; this clustering, cold-tolerant species is among the easiest and fastest-flowering members of the former Notocactus group.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in full sun to bright light in fast-draining cactus mix; this clustering, cold-tolerant species is among the easiest and fastest-flowering members of the former Notocactus group. Native to grasslands of southern Brazil, Uruguay, and northern Argentina, it forms small, flattened-globose, dark green stems armed with fine yellowish spines and offsets readily from the base into low mounded clumps. Large, glossy yellow flowers with a satiny sheen open at the crown from late spring through summer, often produced even on small young plants. More tolerant of cool, humid conditions than many desert cacti, it still needs sharp drainage and a drier winter rest to avoid rot.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in full sun to bright light in fast-draining cactus mix; give this cold-hardy former Notocactus species a dry winter rest to encourage heavy summer flowering.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in full sun to bright light in fast-draining cactus mix; give this cold-hardy former Notocactus species a dry winter rest to encourage heavy summer flowering. Native to Uruguay and adjacent Argentina, it forms a solitary or sparingly clustering, rounded to short-cylindrical stem with prominent ribs lined in stout, dark, downward-curving central spines that stand out against the yellowish-brown spine clusters. Bright yellow flowers open at the crown over an extended period from late spring into summer, often followed by small woolly fruit typical of the group. It handles cooler, more humid summers better than many South American globular cacti but still needs excellent drainage to avoid root rot.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

common_name: Super Kabuto Star Cactus (Dense-Flocked Sand Dollar Cactus)

planting.note: Start seed indoors in warm, humid conditions over a sterile mineral cactus mix; this Japanese-bred seed strain is selected for extra-dense white woolly flecking and takes longer to reach flowering size than the plain species.

directions: Start seed indoors in warm, humid conditions over a sterile mineral cactus mix; this Japanese-bred seed strain is selected for extra-dense white woolly flecking and takes longer to reach flowering size than the plain species. 'Super Kabuto' is a prized selection of the spineless, flattened, ribbed star cactus bred over generations to maximize the size and density of the fuzzy white trichome dots covering its skin, giving mature plants an almost solid white, snowflake-like surface rather than the sparser speckling of wild-type plants. Large yellow flowers with a reddish-orange throat open at the crown in warm weather on established specimens. Because true Super Kabuto plants come from a controlled seed line rather than the endangered wild population, always source seed or plants from reputable specialty growers, and grow in a very gritty, fast-draining mix in full sun to light shade with protection from hard freezes.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining cactus mix; the soft, hooked spines and hairy areoles trap moisture and dust, so water at the soil line rather than overhead.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining cactus mix; the soft, hooked spines and hairy areoles trap moisture and dust, so water at the soil line rather than overhead. Native to the mountains of Durango, Mexico, this small, usually solitary, globose species is covered in dense white silky hair mixed with fine hooked central spines that catch on skin or clothing, softer to the touch than most Mammillaria. It produces disproportionately large, vivid magenta-pink flowers relative to its body size, ringing the crown in mid-spring and among the showiest blooms in the genus. More prone to rot than many Mammillaria if kept too wet or too cool, it does best with a strict dry winter rest and a very lean, mineral soil mix.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

common_name: Old Man Cactus (Mexican Old Man Cactus)

planting.note: Plant in full sun in extremely well-drained, sandy or gravelly soil; this extremely slow-growing columnar cactus is grown almost entirely as a container or greenhouse specimen outside its native frost-free range.

directions: Plant in full sun in extremely well-drained, sandy or gravelly soil; this extremely slow-growing columnar cactus is grown almost entirely as a container or greenhouse specimen outside its native frost-free range. Native to a small area of central Mexico, its single, unbranched, ribbed column is famously draped in long, shaggy, white to yellowish-gray hair that obscures the sharp spines beneath and gives the species its common name, an adaptation thought to help reflect intense high-elevation sunlight and buffer temperature swings. Plants grown from seed take many years to reach even modest height and can live for a century or more in habitat, though flowering rarely occurs in cultivation until the column is quite tall and mature. Keep the hair dry and avoid overhead watering, which mats and discolors it, and protect from any frost, since this species has essentially no cold tolerance.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Start seed indoors in warm conditions over a very lean, mineral cactus mix; always source nursery-propagated seed or plants, since this extremely slow-growing species is heavily poached from the wild and protected across its range.

directions: Start seed indoors in warm conditions over a very lean, mineral cactus mix; always source nursery-propagated seed or plants, since this extremely slow-growing species is heavily poached from the wild and protected across its range. Native to the Chihuahuan Desert of Texas and northern Mexico, it grows nearly flush with the soil as a spineless, gray-brown rosette of thick, warty, fissured tubercles that closely mimic surrounding limestone rock, an extreme camouflage strategy that gives the species its common name. A deep taproot lets it survive long droughts, and pink to magenta daisy-like flowers open from the woolly center in fall, often after the first cool rains. Because it can take a decade or more to reach flowering size, grow it in an unusually gritty, fast-draining mix, water sparingly even in the growing season, and expect a genuinely slow but very long-lived plant.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow in full sun in extremely well-drained, gravelly or sandy soil; this Chihuahuan Desert native tolerates brief light frost when kept dry but rots quickly in wet, poorly drained conditions.

directions: Grow in full sun in extremely well-drained, gravelly or sandy soil; this Chihuahuan Desert native tolerates brief light frost when kept dry but rots quickly in wet, poorly drained conditions. Native to south Texas and northern Mexico, it forms a solitary, cylindrical to egg-shaped, blue-green stem ringed with prominent ribs and banded spines that are often two-toned, typically reddish-pink or purplish near the base of each spine cluster fading to cream or white at the tip. Large, vivid magenta-pink flowers with a darker throat open at the crown in late spring and can reach 3 inches across, disproportionately showy for the plant's modest size. Best grown in a raised bed or container of lean, mineral soil with a dry winter rest, since it is more sensitive to overwatering and humidity than many Texas native cacti.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference
